The western-states deployment, and what we benchmark next

1,306,587,886 phase picks from 12,697 stations, what the campaign did not pick and why, how we score it, and the case for a benchmark organised by earthquake-sequence regime instead of by place.

How these are counted

  • The pick total is read from the footers of 276,741 of the 488,937 Parquet objects that exist, so it is a floor rather than the total. The remaining 212,196 are being counted now.
  • The P and S split is measured on 15,704,001 picks read from 2,616 files stratified across every network, 1.20% of the catalogue, with no failed reads. Applied to the exact total it gives 675,392,574 P and 631,195,312 S.
  • 101,005 shard manifests record 14,103,780 station-days of work, 24,008 station epochs were in scope across 119 networks.

Where the picks came from

11,497 of the 12,880 stations the campaign processed carry coordinates in the campaign station table and produced at least one pick. Circle area follows pick count. The heaviest producers are PB.B934 (13M, California), PB.B943 (13M, Washington), PB.B013 (12M, Washington). Borehole instruments dominate the top of the list: 40% of the twenty largest counts are Plate Boundary Observatory stations, which sit in quiet holes and detect far more than a surface sensor beside them. Coastline and state borders from Natural Earth.

The station-days that produced nothing

14.10M
station-days processed
8.2%
wrote no picks (1,157,258)

A station-day that completes without writing a pick is not always an error. A station can be dead, clipped, or recording nothing a picker will call an arrival. It becomes an error when the worker reports success and the reason is a data-path failure rather than a quiet day, which is the case we have had to chase four times.

183 stations were processed and never produced a single pick across their whole record. Those are the ones to look at first.

Do the manifests and the Parquet agree?

manifests say workers wrote1,737,169,720
Parquet footers read so far1,306,587,886
objects counted276,741 of 488,937

These two are not yet comparable. The manifests cover the whole campaign; the footers cover 57% of the objects. The count is running and the answer belongs on this slide, not an estimate.

What the comparison is for

  • The manifests are what the workers reported writing. The footers are what is actually in the bucket. A gap in either direction is a defect: picks that never landed, or manifests that over-report.
  • We have found four ways a station-day can be reported as done without its output surviving. The largest, resumed shards overwriting their own output, cost 25.3M picks before it was fixed. This comparison is how we would see a fifth.
  • The dashboard's cached footer count stops on the clock each run, so it holds 276,741 of 488,937 objects and its headline should not be quoted as the catalogue size.
  • Whatever the answer, it does not move a benchmark result: those are scored on waveforms re-picked from the archive, not on the catalogue.

Offshore is not in this catalogue

Ocean-bottom stations off the western states live in the obs/ partition of the bucket, not in western/.

The split is deliberate. OBS records need a different weight set (obs, PickBlue), they carry a hydrophone channel the land models do not read, and their reference arrivals come from different sources. Scoring them against the land benchmark would mix two questions.

Anyone reading the western catalogue for a coastal study should know that the offshore instruments are a separate read: s3://quakescope-picks-2026/obs/picks/.

What we score a picker on

Our reference is an operator bulletin, not a labelled test set. An analyst picked what a location needed and stopped, so an unmatched model pick may be a false positive or a real arrival nobody marked. That one fact decides which metrics mean anything.

metricagainst a bulletin
Recallexact
Picks emittedexact
Onset MAE, RMSE, MedianAE, biasexact
Gross-error rateexact
P/S swap rate (association)exact
Duplicate picksexact
Precision, F1lower bound
Calibration, ECElower bound
MCCnot computable

Three ways to set the threshold

A confidence of 0.3 from one model and 0.3 from another are not the same operating point, so the protocol decides the ranking:

  • One shared threshold. What most comparisons report. It measures how willing a model is to emit a pick as much as how well it picks.
  • Equal pick count. Threshold-free, but the count all models can reach is capped by the most conservative one.
  • Each model's own threshold. What a tuned deployment would run. No held-out split, so it is an upper bound.

Residuals are matched at 2 s and detection at 0.5 s: matching at the detection tolerance truncates the residual distribution and makes an outlier rate a statement about the tolerance.

quakescope2026, our own fine-tune, ranks 1 of 4 on its own region and 4 of 4 outside it. A pooled number hides that, because the out-of-region track carries most of the reference arrivals. On track 2 the recall leader is also the least accurate on onset time, so a catalogue built for locations and one built for completeness do not want the same weights. Full board: seisscoped.org/QuakeScope/benchmark_metrics.html

Place-based benchmarks run out

Every sequence we score is a place, and the training corpora are places too.

  • INSTANCE holds Etna and Campi Flegrei from 2005 to 2020. VCSEIS holds Alaska, Hawaii, northern California and the Cascades. CREW is global at regional distance. A benchmark drawn from the same places measures memory of a place.
  • Holding out a time window at a known place leaves that place's earlier years in training. Volcanoes and swarms recur at the same place, so for those the hold-out has to be the place itself, at all times, and the cost in training data has to be accepted.
  • Our sequences are also all mainshock-aftershock. Seven of eight on the current board are a cascade or a doublet. A picker that handles an aftershock cascade has not been shown to handle a swarm migrating for months.

What a catalogue actually has to survive

regimewhat breaks
Mainshock-aftershockevents seconds apart, overlapping codas, a saturating network
Volcano-tectonicemergent onsets, low magnitudes, long-period events a picker was never trained on
Fluid-driven swarmmonths of elevated rate, no mainshock, shallow sources and a dense local array

These are different failure modes, not different places. Scoring by regime is what tells a deployment which one it is buying.

Why not reuse the curated sets

The benchmark we have is 35,392 single-arrival windows from 12 SeisBench datasets (instancecounts 9,776, stead 9,360, ceed 5,435, pnw 2,841, txed 2,261, and 7 more). One pick per window, no sequence context, and every one of those datasets is in the fine-tune's training manifest. It measures timing on isolated arrivals and cannot measure generalisation, so it stays as a unit test.

What the regime set is instead

Continuous data scored at the event level against picks an operator or a published study made by hand, on sequences drawn from bulletins rather than from any curated corpus. 12 of 21 are scorable now. The rest fail on the reference, not the model: a bulletin that under-collects, or station codes that resolve to one station. Still missing: a sequence that postdates the training window of every model it scores, labelled independently.
